clue.text: Usual thing, article featuring Greg? Of course

parts.note: the norm is the usual or standard thing
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A puzzled aside about a newspaper article that features someone called Greg, answered with a confident 'of course'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as an interjection, but it hints at a golf course: Greg Norman is the Australian golfer.
explanation.definitionFit: Surname of the Australian golfer Greg, a star of the golf course, hence the punning question mark.

clue.text: Carefully observe lack of label, the main mistake ultimately

parts.note: no means none of, a lack of
a tab is a small label or tag

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: A warning to watch out for a missing label, the chief error in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes the last letters of 'the', 'main' and 'mistake', giving E, N, E.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase, abbreviated NB, is an instruction to take careful notice of something.

clue.text: Cart seen struggling in second climb

indicators.note: struggling suggests the letters of the two words are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A cart is seen labouring on a second ascent of a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: A further ascent: going up again is a second climb.

clue.text: Leading character needing drink heads for public house

parts.note: ale is beer, a drink

indicators.note: heads for picks out the first letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A leading actor needs a pint and heads for the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads for' takes the initials of 'public house', P and H (also the abbreviation PH for a pub).
explanation.definitionFit: First letter of the Hebrew alphabet, so it leads all the other characters.

clue.text: Barrier standard gets vocal support

parts.note: stock as an adjective means standard, regular

indicators.note: vocal says the word for support is to be taken as spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: aid is help or support

explanation.surface: A standard barrier is given spoken backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vocal' turns AID into ADE, which sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence of upright posts built as a defensive enclosure is a kind of barrier.

clue.text: Help win there, I ordered, issuing this?

definitions.text: Help win there, I ordered, issuing this?

indicators.note: ordered says the letters are put into a new order, while also being the command in the surface

explanation.surface: A party whip demands support to win a vote and gives the strongest possible instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges HELPWINTHEREI. The whole clue also describes the instruction a party whip issues before a crucial vote.
explanation.definitionFit: In UK parliamentary jargon, the most urgent summons from a party whip, underlined three times, demanding members attend and vote.

clue.text: Actors with a gun in send-up — they click

parts.note: the cast are the actors in a production

indicators.note: in a down clue, sent up means written upwards, so the word for gun reads in reverse

parts.note: the Sten is a British submachine gun

explanation.surface: A troupe of actors brandish a gun in a comic parody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in send-up' reverses STEN to NETS; a send-up looks like a spoof here.
explanation.definitionFit: Pairs of wooden shells clicked together in the hand by flamenco dancers.

clue.text: Saudi, perhaps, supported by the French, providing food

indicators.note: in a down clue, being supported by means the next piece sits underneath

parts.note: a Saudi is an example of an Arab
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A Saudi backed by the French is providing food aid.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes land suitable for growing crops, so it is farmland that yields food.

clue.text: Anger after Eastern politician's found in powerful organisation

indicators.note: after places the word for anger behind the other pieces

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament
ire is anger

explanation.surface: An Eastern politician's rage is discovered inside a mighty organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, a large business group under one controlling person, a commercial realm with great power.

clue.text: Narrator covering artist, very peripatetic one

indicators.note: covering means the word for narrator goes round the other letters

parts.note: a teller tells a story, a narrator
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A storyteller covers an artist who is constantly on the move.
explanation.definitionFit: Peripatetic means travelling from place to place, so a peripatetic person is one who journeys.

clue.text: Largely unconvincing, girl and Dad brought over material — see boss here

indicators.note: in a down clue, Dad brought over the material means placed on top of it
largely means most but not all of the word, dropping its last letter

parts.note: a lame excuse is an unconvincing one
Beth is a girl's name
pa is dad
lace is a fabric, material

explanation.surface: An unconvincing tale about a girl and her father fetching fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Largely' drops the last letter of LAME. A see is a bishop's diocese; this is the London residence of the Archbishop of Canterbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Official London residence where the Archbishop of Canterbury, head of that bishop's see, lives.

clue.text: Little change after swindle — the rascal!

indicators.note: after puts the coin after the swindle

parts.note: a scam is a swindle
p, a penny, is a small coin, little change

explanation.surface: An exclamation at someone who pocketed a little change after a con.
explanation.definitionFit: A mischievous child or rogue is a scallywag or rascal.

clue.text: Footballer's signal — touching part of leg?

definitions.note: read as Footballer is, the definition is the footballer

parts.note: a beck is a gesture or signal, as in beck and call
the ham is the back of the thigh

explanation.surface: A footballer gives a signal by touching part of his leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touching' just places the pieces next to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: David, the famous England football captain, bears this surname.

clue.text: At end of race, Bannister, say, hugging a communicator?

indicators.note: at end of picks out the final letter of race
hugging means the runner wraps round the letter a

parts.note: Roger Bannister, the first to run a four-minute mile, is an example of a miler

explanation.surface: At the end of a race Roger Bannister is hugging someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Bannister ran the first sub-four-minute mile in 1954.
explanation.definitionFit: One who sends electronic messages is a communicator of a modern kind, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Unfortunate internee who's kept in dark?

indicators.note: unfortunate suggests the letters have come to grief and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pitiable prisoner held in the dark.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for still not understanding or knowing more, as someone deprived of information is.

clue.text: When June finishes, as do three "colleagues"

definitions.text: When June finishes, as do three "colleagues"

parts.words: When June finishes, as do three "colleagues"
parts.note: June ends on its final, thirty-day date, and so do its 'colleagues' April, September and November

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November' supplies the three other months.
explanation.definitionFit: The ordinal date on which every thirty-day month closes, June and its three fellows alike.

clue.text: Blame at expected level over extremely elusive old Irish robber

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the earlier pieces above the next

parts.note: to take the rap is to take the blame
par is the expected or normal level

indicators.note: extremely takes the extreme letters, first and last, of elusive

explanation.surface: Blame for an elusive old Irish robber stays at the expected level.
explanation.definitionFit: Historical term for a seventeenth-century Irish irregular soldier or freebooter, later any bandit.

clue.text: Bottom daughter to slip up? That is right — on drug

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the earlier piece sits on top of the next

parts.note: to err is to slip up
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
E is ecstasy, a drug

explanation.surface: A daughter at the bottom of the class makes a mistake while on drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A coy, French-derived euphemism for the buttocks, the backside.

clue.text: Well-off saying little about Western state's seismic measure?

parts.note: to be well-off is to be rich

indicators.note: about means the brief word goes around the state

parts.note: terse means brief, saying little
Cal abbreviates California, a western US state

explanation.surface: A wealthy person says little about a Western state's earthquake measure.
explanation.definitionFit: A logarithmic gauge of earthquake magnitude devised by Charles Richter, the classic seismic yardstick.

clue.text: Crush spirit

definitions.meaning: to stamp out or put an end to, as in quashing a rumour

explanation.definitionFit: One word means to quash or stamp out; it is also whisky from Scotland.

clue.text: Very African country? Not this person's

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
Mali is a West African country

explanation.surface: A question about an African country, answered: not this person's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'African country' looks like one piece, but 'country' alone gives MALI; the tag 'Not this person's' points out that Mali is not the country of the person meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Somalia, in the Horn of Africa, is an African.

clue.text: Country air — coat needs changing

indicators.note: needs changing says the letters must be altered into a new order

explanation.surface: Country air means a coat needs changing.
explanation.definitionFit: A Balkan nation on the Adriatic coast is a country.

clue.text: Harry Tottenham follower?

definitions.meaning: Harry Percy, the fiery nobleman nicknamed in Shakespeare's Henry IV
the word that follows Tottenham in the London football club's name

explanation.walkthrough: Tottenham Hotspur is a London football club; 'follower' looks like a fan but means the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Nickname of Sir Henry Percy, Shakespeare's Harry; also the second word of Tottenham's football club name.

clue.text: Taking time, chap with tips from feminist

parts.note: he is a male, a chap

indicators.note: tips from takes the two end letters of feminist

explanation.surface: A chap takes his time, with pointers from a feminist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tips from' gives F and T, the ends of 'feminist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealing is the illicit taking of property, so the noun matches the gerund.

clue.text: Type of war speech I rejected

indicators.note: rejected means the letter I is cast out of the speech

parts.note: a tirade is a long angry speech

explanation.surface: Someone rejects a speech about a particular kind of war.
explanation.definitionFit: A tariff battle between nations is called a trade war, so the word names that type.

clue.text: A very quiet rental property always on reflection a fruitful source

parts.note: pp, pianissimo, is the musical mark for very quiet
a let is a property rented out

indicators.note: on reflection means the word for always is mirrored, read backwards

parts.note: e'er is a poetic contraction of ever, always

explanation.surface: A very quiet rental property always turns out a fruitful source of income, on reflection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' reverses EER (e'er, poetic for 'ever') to REE.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchard tree bearing pippins is literally a source of fruit.

clue.text: Female boxing crew to become more intense?

indicators.note: boxing means the female encloses the crew

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
an eight is a rowing crew

explanation.surface: A female boxing a rowing crew makes things more intense.
explanation.definitionFit: To intensify or increase, as tension rises and grows stronger.

clue.text: In auditorium, source of strength, old rocker Tommy?

indicators.note: in an auditorium words are heard, so the word for strength is taken by its sound

parts.note: steel is proverbially a source of strength

explanation.surface: In a concert hall, an old rock and roller is a source of strength.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy Steele was an early British rock and roll star.
explanation.definitionFit: Surname of Tommy, Britain's first teen rock 'n' roll idol in the 1950s.
